A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DP-FUSION research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original TAB-ECHR experiments measuring perplexity, paraphrase win rates, token-recovery attack success, and privacy accounting, with further results in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original candidate-set, tagging, single-group, medical-document, and prompt-injection evaluations in its appendices.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same inference, mollification, averaging, and sampling procedure. Appendix A.18 describes single-group inference as its existing m=1 specialization, but states a one-sided Rényi constraint where Algorithm 1 requires a symmetric constraint. The PDFs do not resolve whether this discrepancy represents an implemented procedural change or a documentation error.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained legal-document task, v2 evaluates medical-document privatization on 181 MACCROBAT documents and prompt injection using 100 HotpotQA question-context pairs. It also tests operation with imperfect automatic annotations instead of exclusively gold privacy labels. These substantially broaden domains and operating scenarios.

E2.justification: The retained comparisons still evaluate DP-Prompt, DP-Decoding, and public/original-document paraphrasing controls. Added settings reuse these controls or undefended inference without introducing a new competing defense algorithm. BERT-NER, spaCy, and Flair are evaluated tagging components rather than competing DP-FUSION defenses.

E3.justification: New protocols include single-group configurations with larger divergence bounds, candidate-set sizes from 3 to 10, and embedding cosine similarity as an additional utility metric. The RAG evaluation constructs 1,000 adversarial pairs and defines success as verbatim reproduction of injected text. The original main comparison retains its settings; these are additional evaluations.

E4.justification: V2 adds candidate-set sensitivity analysis, measurements of tagging errors, end-to-end comparisons using imperfect taggers, single-group trade-off analysis, and robustness testing against poisoned retrieval chunks. These address previously untested practical assumptions. V1's divergence and privacy-accounting analyses remain present after relocation.

E5.justification: The existing 95% confidence intervals for mean divergence and Wilson intervals for binned attack success are retained. The reference to multiple runs also remains. V2 does not establish a new repeated-run, seed, significance-testing, or uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the corresponding original full-result tables retain their values. New Table 9 reports BERT-NER-based DP-FUSION at αβ=0.01 achieving 38.3% ASR and 0.764 cosine similarity, versus 51.2% and 0.743 for its public baseline. Tables 12–13 add medical and injection results. Table 13 reports 0% ASR at the three tightest bounds versus an undefended mean of 51.2%; 90% is the maximum for one injection. These are newly reported settings, not improvements to the original benchmark scores.

T1.justification: The principal definitions, transcript privacy bound, and monotonicity proof are retained. V2 removes v1's short argument extending monotonicity to symmetric divergence. Appendix A.18 additionally states a one-sided single-group constraint while claiming the same accountant, without reconciling it with Algorithm 1's symmetric constraint.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion now present mitigation of prompt injection as a contribution, extending the original privacy-leakage claims to controlling malicious retrieved instructions. The new sixfold-perplexity headline quantifies evidence already present in v1 rather than reflecting changed original results.

C2.justification: V2 substantially revises the discussion to distinguish tagged-span guarantee validity from tagging coverage, interpret false positives and negatives, and explain grouping and data-density effects on utility. It adds a hypothesis about weakened safety alignment at loose bounds. V1's extended discussion of cross-group dependence and unintuitive privacy-budget selection is reduced, although the independence assumption remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds exact tagger identifiers, a detection threshold, the sentence-embedding model, detailed dataset statistics, and the RAG injection template. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit code/data availability link, FP16 specification, 10,000-character input limit, and random-subset selection description. These alter reproducibility documentation; the missing link does not establish that resources became unavailable.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially toward practical PII tagging and RAG poisoning/jailbreak defenses, with additions including Presidio, Pham et al., Deng et al., Liu et al., and Zou et al. Several earlier background references are removed. The foundational relationship to PMixED, PATE, and SUBMIX remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The experimental narrative is condensed and reorganized, while separate appendices A–N become subsections A.1–A.21. Former main-text divergence analyses move into the appendix. This exceeds local copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is replaced and placed within the introduction. Numerous retained figures are resized or relocated, including diagnostic plots moved into the appendix. New candidate-set and utility plots, dataset-statistics tables, and tagging, medical, and injection-result tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: The real-tagger experiments directly test v1's acknowledged oracle limitation, while candidate-set and medical analyses strengthen empirical support for practical applicability. These gains are partly offset by removed reproducibility disclosures and the inconsistent single-group constraint. The new security claims also exceed Appendix A.20's known-poisoned-chunk, verbatim-reproduction evaluation, which reports no answer-quality trade-off. Together, these support a limited net improvement.
